title: The Chimes
author: Charles Dickens
setting: London on the last day of an old year, from a porter's post outside a church to the bell tower above it, with a vision that runs years ahead
lengthNote: Four Quarters, about 30,000 words, named after the chimes a church clock rings at each quarter of the hour
openingLine: There are not many people—and as it is desirable that a story-teller and a story-reader should establish a mutual understanding as soon as possible, I beg it to be noticed that I confine this observation neither to young people nor to little people, but extend it to all conditions of people: little and big, young and old: yet growing up, or already growing down again—there are not, I say, many people who would care to sleep in a church.
summary: Toby Veck, known as Trotty, is an old ticket-porter who waits for errands outside a London church. On the last day of the year he listens to gentlemen with statistics and opinions explain what is wrong with the poor, and by nightfall he has come to agree with them. The church bells then call him up the tower and show him what those opinions do to his daughter Meg over the years that follow. He wakes as the bells ring in the New Year, which is also her wedding day.
referenceStyle: quarter, following the four divisions Dickens named after a clock's quarter chimes

sourceText.label: Project Gutenberg text of The Chimes (eBook 653)
sourceText.note: Transcribed by David Price from the Charles Scribner's Sons edition of the Works of Charles Dickens. References give the Quarter, the only division the book uses. Dialect spellings such as Trotty's 'obserwation' and Will Fern's 'creeturs' are quoted as printed.

atAGlance.label: Published
atAGlance.note: Dickens's second Christmas book, a year after A Christmas Carol.

atAGlance.label: Subtitle
atAGlance.note: In full, A Goblin Story of Some Bells that Rang an Old Year Out and a New Year In.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: Dickens was living in Genoa that year, and his letters from the city mention the bells he heard there.

atAGlance.label: Divisions
atAGlance.note: First Quarter to Fourth Quarter are Dickens's own names for the parts, taken from the chimes of a church clock.

atAGlance.label: Time span
atAGlance.note: The waking story runs from Trotty's dinner-time to the New Year peal. The vision inside it covers nine years and more.

structure.label: First Quarter
structure.title: Tripe on the church steps
structure.summary: Trotty stands at his post in the cold, wondering aloud whether the poor are born bad. Meg brings him hot tripe and the news that Richard wants to marry her on New Year's Day, since waiting will only make them old. Three gentlemen come out of the house whose steps they are eating on. Filer proves by arithmetic that tripe is wasteful, a red-faced gentleman mourns the good old times, and Alderman Cute tells Meg he will Put Down her troubles before she has had them. The couple leave apart, and the bells seem to ring the gentlemen's phrases.

scenes.summary: The narrator's opening about sleeping alone in a church, Trotty's niche in the church wall, and his belief that the bells talk to him.
A guessing game over a basin of tripe, and Meg's report of Richard's argument that the poor who wait for better times wait for the grave.
Filer's figures, the good old times, and Cute's promise to Put Down distressed wives, shoeless boys and suicide.
Cute pays Trotty sixpence to carry a letter, and the bells, which used to tell him to keep a good heart, now repeat the gentlemen.

structure.label: Second Quarter
structure.title: The Poor Man's Friend
structure.summary: Trotty carries Cute's letter to Sir Joseph Bowley, a Member of Parliament who settles every account before the year turns and calls himself the Poor Man's Friend and Father. The letter asks whether Will Fern, a labourer from Sir Joseph's village found asleep in a shed, should be put down, and Sir Joseph dictates a reply recommending prison. On the way home Trotty runs into Fern himself, carrying his orphaned niece Lilian, warns him off, and takes them both home to Meg. Alone later with his newspaper, he reads of a mother who killed herself and her child, decides the poor really are bad, and hears the bells calling him up the tower.

scenes.summary: A charity that gives two votes for five pounds, a full-length portrait over the fireplace, and a letter asking for Fern's committal as a vagabond.
Trotty admits to owing Mrs Chickenstalker ten or twelve shillings and a little rent, and is sent away as an example of his class.
A countryman explains, without raising his voice, why he wants the gentry to leave him alone, and Trotty carries his niece home.
The newspaper, the bells ringing 'Haunt and hunt him', and a climb in the dark until Trotty faints among the bells.

structure.label: Third Quarter
structure.title: The Goblin Sight
structure.summary: Trotty comes round in a belfry swarming with spirits of the bells. The Goblin of the Great Bell charges him with wronging the Chimes, above all by hearing in them the creed of the men who would put the poor down, and a spirit with the face of the child Lilian becomes his guide. He sees his own body at the foot of the tower, nine years dead. He then watches Meg and the grown Lilian sewing for bare bread, a New Year's Day banquet at Bowley Hall interrupted by Will Fern fresh from prison, Richard come to Meg ruined by drink, and Lilian's return to die at Meg's knees.

scenes.summary: Spirits pour out of the bells and die away when the ringing stops, and the Great Bell lists the wrongs Trotty has done in words.
Two women at their needlework, and Lilian asking to be made old so that her youth cannot tempt her.
Skittles with the tenants, news that the banker Deedles has shot himself, and Will Fern's speech to the gentry.
Richard brings a purse from Lilian that Meg will not touch. Later Lilian comes back herself and dies asking to be forgiven.

structure.label: Fourth Quarter
structure.title: To desperation
structure.summary: More years pass in the vision. Mrs Chickenstalker has married Tugby, Sir Joseph's former porter, and Meg lodges above their shop, married at last to Richard in the hope of saving him. Richard dies and leaves her with a baby girl. Will Fern visits her for the last time and speaks of fires to come, and on the last night of the year Tugby turns her out. She carries the baby to the river, and Trotty, crying that he has learnt his lesson, holds her back as the New Year bells break the vision. He wakes to find Meg trimming her gown for the wedding and Richard at the door, and the neighbours arrive with a band.

scenes.summary: Mrs Tugby tells a doctor who attends the poor how Meg came to marry Richard, and Richard dies upstairs.
Fern holds the baby, learns her name, and leaves Meg repeating 'Like Lilian, when her mother died and left her'.
Turned away by Tugby, Meg runs to the water with the child, and Trotty pleads for her to the figures in the bells.
Richard claims the first kiss of the year, the Drum brings a band, and Mrs Chickenstalker turns out to be the friend Will Fern came to London to find.

characters.name: Toby Veck (Trotty)
characters.summary: An old porter, over sixty, who stands outside a London church waiting for errands and is called Trotty from his pace. He loves earning his money and wants to believe he is worth his salt, which is why the gentlemen's talk hurts him: he takes it seriously. The book follows how he comes to think that people like him are born bad, and how hard it is for him to unlearn it.
characters.clue: He eats tripe on a stranger's doorstep, hears the bells tell him to keep a good heart, and spends the sixpence the Alderman paid him on tea and bacon for a guest.

characters.name: Meg Veck
characters.summary: Trotty's only child, whose mother died when she was small. She brings her father his dinner, plans a New Year's Day wedding with Richard, and is frightened out of it by one speech from Alderman Cute. In the vision she becomes the test case for the gentlemen's theories, worked and starved over years until she carries her baby to the river.
characters.clue: She makes her father guess what is in the basin, spreads a pocket-handkerchief for a tablecloth, and in the vision gives her baby her own name.

relationships.label: shelters and loves like a sister

characters.name: Richard
characters.role: A young smith, engaged to Meg
characters.summary: A strong, handsome young smith who argues that the poor cannot afford to wait for better times, because waiting leads only to the grave. In the vision he takes the gentlemen's hint that he could do better than Meg, loses his work, looks and friends to drink, and marries her too late to be saved. Awake, he wants to answer the Alderman back, and Meg will not let him.
characters.clue: His face glows like the iron he hammers, and he waits outside Trotty's door to claim the first kiss of the New Year.

characters.name: Will Fern
characters.role: A labourer from Sir Joseph Bowley's village
characters.summary: A sun-browned countryman with grizzled hair who has walked to London to look for work and for a friend of Lilian's dead mother, carrying the child in his arms. He talks about a working life that never kept him without heat or self-pity. In the vision he comes out of jail again and again, until he visits Meg to say goodbye and speaks of fires in the dark.
characters.clue: He winds his niece's hair round his finger like a ring, and tells a banquet of gentlefolk that they have drunk the health of the Labourer.

relationships.label: is lodged for a night by
is marked for putting down by
finds the friend he was seeking in

characters.name: Lilian Fern
characters.summary: A child of nine when Trotty carries her home, and in the vision a young woman sewing beside Meg for bare bread. She asks Meg to make her old so that she will not be tempted, and later sends money through Richard from a life the book describes only by what it has cost her. The Spirit of the Chimes that guides Trotty wears her face as a child.
characters.clue: She falls asleep holding Meg's hand, and years later dies on her knees in front of her, asking to be forgiven.

relationships.label: appears to as the Spirit of the Chimes

characters.name: Alderman Cute
characters.role: Alderman and Justice of the Peace
characters.summary: A merry, knowing magistrate who is sure he understands the common people and means to Put Down whatever troubles him about them, from want and starvation to young mothers and suicide. When a rich banker shoots himself, he talks instead about nerves and the mysteries of the machine called Man.
characters.clue: He finishes Trotty's tripe himself, tells Meg her sons will grow up bad, and chucks her under the chin.

characters.name: Mr Filer
characters.summary: A low-spirited gentleman who reduces everything to tables. He is so short-sighted that he has to put his face almost into Trotty's tripe to see what it is, which is Dickens's joke about how closely he looks at the poor. He calculates the waste on tripe until Trotty feels he has starved a garrison, and declares that the poor have no more right to marry than to be born.
characters.clue: He prods a piece of tripe with a pencil-case, divides the nation's supply among its widows and orphans, and says four prison terms is over the average.

relationships.label: leads the party Sir Joseph disowns

characters.name: Sir Joseph Bowley
characters.summary: The self-appointed Poor Man's Friend and Father, who settles every account before the year turns and tells Trotty that his only business in life is with Sir Joseph. He says he agrees with no party, then signs a letter asking Cute to commit Will Fern as a vagabond. In the vision he gives a banquet for his tenants on his wife's birthday and toasts the Dignity of Labour.
characters.clue: He keeps a secretary with a cheque-book at his elbow, a full-length portrait of himself over the fireplace, and a skittle match for his tenants.

relationships.label: calls himself the friend and father of

characters.name: Mrs Chickenstalker
characters.role: A shopkeeper in the general line
characters.summary: A stout widow with a crowded little shop, to whom Trotty owes ten or twelve shillings. In the vision she has married Tugby, Sir Joseph's former porter, and she stands up for Meg against a husband who wants the dying Richard sent to the workhouse. In the waking ending she arrives with a steaming pitcher of flip and turns out to have been the friend of Lilian's mother.
characters.clue: Her husband's name replaces hers over the shop door, and she threatens to leave him sooner than turn Meg out.

relationships.label: was a friend of the mother of

characters.name: The Goblin of the Great Bell
characters.role: The spirit of the largest bell in the tower
characters.summary: A bearded, hooded figure the size of its bell, which speaks for all the Chimes. It tries Trotty for the wrongs he has done them in words and sends him to learn from his daughter's life how bad the bad are born, a sentence that turns out to mean the reverse of what Trotty first hears in it.
characters.clue: It rests on nothing, holds a muffled hand to its mouth, and puts Trotty on trial for the wrongs he has done in words.

themes.name: Who speaks for the poor
themes.summary: Every powerful man in the book has a theory of the poor, and none of them asks a poor person anything. Filer has tables, Cute has a phrase, Sir Joseph has a paternal system and the red-faced gentleman has a lost golden age. Will Fern is the one labourer given a platform, and he uses it first to ask the gentry to leave him alone and then to ask for better homes, food and laws.
themes.development: The theories are set out as talk in the first two Quarters. The vision in the third and fourth shows them applied to Meg, Lilian, Richard and Fern over years.

themes.name: Born bad
themes.summary: Trotty's question at noon is whether the poor are born bad or have been made to feel that they are. The gentlemen answer it for him, a newspaper story seems to confirm the answer, and the vision exists to reverse it: Meg, the best person he knows, is driven towards the act he called unnatural that evening.
themes.development: A doubt in the First Quarter, a conviction by the end of the Second, and a retraction at the river, where Trotty pleads that the crime has sprung from 'Love perverted'.

themes.name: Putting down
themes.summary: Alderman Cute’s favourite phrase treats punishment as social policy: whatever is inconvenient about poverty can be removed by a magistrate. Dickens tests it on Will Fern, jailed for sleeping in a shed and then for almost every attempt to live, and on the banker Deedles, who shoots himself and is mourned by Cute as the most respectable of men.
themes.development: Threatened in the First Quarter, rung by the bells, described from the receiving end in Fern's speech at Bowley Hall, and exposed by the Deedles episode, which it never reaches.

themes.name: The right to marry
themes.summary: Richard and Meg want to marry because waiting will only make them old. Filer calls that ignorance of political economy and Cute calls it unbecoming, and in the vision their advice works: the engagement lingers and breaks, and the marriage that finally happens is a rescue attempt. The book ends with the wedding restored to New Year's Day and a band in the room.
themes.development: Proposed at noon, talked out of existence by the gentlemen, shown failing across the vision, and reinstated in the last pages.

themes.name: The Old Year and the New
themes.summary: The story runs from noon to midnight on the last day of a year, and its clock is audible throughout: dinner-time, the quarter chimes, the old year dying like a worn-out labourer, the New Year awaited like an heir. The Goblin speaks for Time and tells Trotty that lamenting the good old times is a wrong done to it.
themes.development: The Second Quarter makes the dying year an allegory of an old working man. The Third makes Time a force that cries Advance. The Fourth ends in the New Year peal and Trotty's prophecy of a sea of Time that will sweep oppressors away.

themes.name: The Dignity of Labour
themes.summary: Trotty loves to earn his money, and Fern says he never held his hand back from work however hard or poorly paid. Sir Joseph toasts the Dignity of Labour at a banquet his tenants are let into after eating their puddings in another hall. Meg and Lilian's needlework shows what the phrase means in practice: long nights of work that earn only enough to go on working.
themes.development: Praised as a principle in Sir Joseph's library, toasted at Bowley Hall, and measured in the vision by what Meg can earn with a baby in her lap.

themes.name: Respectable men
themes.summary: The book saves the word for the rich. Deedles, who puts a pistol to his mouth in his own counting house, is 'one of the most respectable men' Cute ever knew, while the poor mother in Trotty's newspaper is unnatural and cruel. At that point the narrator breaks in and asks Cute to weigh the two cases on his own scales.
themes.development: Sir Joseph's settled accounts set the standard in the Second Quarter; Deedles breaks it in the Third; Tugby, a 'retail Friend and Father', applies it to Meg in the Fourth.

techniques.name: Mock praise
techniques.definition: Praising a character in terms that condemn him.
techniques.inThisBook: Whenever Alderman Cute is at his worst, the narrator adds a line of applause in the voice of his admirers: famous man for the common people, always affable with the working classes, not a bit of pride. The praise comes straight after his cruellest remarks, so the reader does the judging.

techniques.name: The bells' burden
techniques.definition: A phrase repeated at intervals so that its meaning shifts with what has happened since.
techniques.inThisBook: Trotty hears the bells say 'keep a good heart', then 'Put 'em down' and 'Facts and Figures', then 'Haunt and hunt him', then 'Follow her' and 'To desperation'. The bells keep one rhythm and Trotty fits whatever he fears into it. His own refrain, 'Here we are and here we go', belongs to his moments of generosity.

techniques.name: Bells and years as people
techniques.definition: Objects and abstractions given bodies, voices and feelings.
techniques.inThisBook: The bells were baptised by bishops and had godfathers; the old year lies down to die like a labourer who has done his work; the New Year is an infant heir. Dickens gives the calendar a class structure, and the Goblin of the Great Bell, speaking for Time, grows out of the same habit.

techniques.name: Dialect and the right to speak
techniques.definition: Spelling and grammar used to mark where a speaker comes from.
techniques.inThisBook: Trotty says 'obserwation' and 'creetur', and Will Fern speaks a country English ('I has a nat'ral angry word with that man') that the gentlemen would hear as ignorance. Dickens gives Fern the most coherent argument in the book in that dialect, while Sir Joseph flounders for words in his own library.

techniques.name: The storyteller's appeal
techniques.definition: A narrator turning to speak to the reader directly.
techniques.inThisBook: The first sentence asks for a 'mutual understanding' between story-teller and story-reader, and the last paragraph turns to the 'listener' and asks for something to be done in the reader's own sphere. In between, the narrator interrupts to rebuke Cute and to call on 'Youth and Beauty' to look at Lilian.

techniques.name: Dream frame
techniques.definition: A story told as a vision or dream, from which the dreamer wakes.
techniques.inThisBook: Trotty climbs the tower and faints, yet at the end he catches his feet in the newspaper that has fallen on his hearth, as if he had never left his chair. The last paragraph asks whether he dreamed and leaves the question open, while insisting that the 'stern realities' behind the shadows are real.

quotations.text: They hung there, in all weathers, with the wind and rain driving in upon them; facing only the outsides of all those houses; never getting any nearer to the blazing fires that gleamed and shone upon the windows
quotations.context: The narrator explains why Trotty feels a kinship with the bells.
quotations.analysis: Every clause describes Trotty's working day as well as the bells': out in the weather, looking at other people's fires through their windows. Dickens builds the likeness before any goblin appears, so that when the bells start to speak the reader already suspects they are speaking with Trotty's voice.

quotations.text: I get so puzzled sometimes that I am not even able to make up my mind whether there is any good at all in us, or whether we are born bad. We seem to be dreadful things; we seem to give a deal of trouble; we are always being complained of and guarded against. One way or other, we fill the papers.
quotations.speaker: Trotty
quotations.context: Trotty talking to himself outside the church before Meg arrives.
quotations.analysis: He says 'we' throughout, so the doubt is about a class and not about himself. His phrases, 'complained of and guarded against' and 'we fill the papers', are the language in which the poor are written about, and the book's argument starts here: Trotty has learnt his opinion of himself from newspapers.

quotations.text: He says that if we wait: people in our condition: until we see our way quite clearly, the way will be a narrow one indeed—the common way—the Grave, father.
quotations.speaker: Meg, reporting Richard
quotations.context: Meg tells her father why Richard wants them to marry on New Year's Day.
quotations.analysis: Richard's reasoning is economic, and it answers Filer before Filer has spoken: if the poor wait for security before they marry, the only certain thing ahead of them is the grave. The word 'way' shifts three times in the sentence, from a clear view of the future to a narrow path to the road everybody takes. Meg delivers it 'in a tremble, but quite plainly'.

quotations.text: and may heap up facts on figures, facts on figures, facts on figures, mountains high and dry; and he can no more hope to persuade ’em that they have no right or business to be married, than he can hope to persuade ’em that they have no earthly right or business to be born.
quotations.speaker: Mr Filer
quotations.context: Filer's reply when Richard says he and Meg will be married on New Year's Day.
quotations.analysis: The sentence moves from marrying to being born as if the second followed obviously from the first, and Filer adds that the point was 'reduced to a mathematical certainty long ago'. He has just divided the nation's tripe by its widows and orphans to reach a pennyweight each. Dickens lets the argument run in its own terms until the terms condemn it: a couple are told their existence was an error in the sums.

quotations.text: Famous man for the common people, Alderman Cute! Never out of temper with them! Easy, affable, joking, knowing gentleman!
quotations.context: The narrator's comment after Cute boasts that it is easy to deal with 'this sort of people' if you understand them.
quotations.analysis: These lines have no main verb and no named speaker, and they sound like Cute's reputation talking. Dickens repeats the trick each time the Alderman is at his worst, with 'Always affable with the working classes' and 'O, he knew how to banter the common people', until the praise has become an accusation the narrator never has to make outright.

quotations.text: And if you attempt, desperately, and ungratefully, and impiously, and fraudulently attempt, to drown yourself, or hang yourself, I’ll have no pity for you, for I have made up my mind to Put all suicide Down!
quotations.speaker: Alderman Cute
quotations.context: The end of Cute's advice to Meg on the day she has agreed to marry.
quotations.analysis: Four adverbs pile moral charges on an act of despair, and 'fraudulently' is the oddest of them, as if a starving woman who tried to drown herself were cheating someone. Cute says all this to a girl planning her wedding, cheerfully and in public. The Fourth Quarter sends Meg to the river his speech describes.

quotations.text: Put ’em down, Put ’em down! Good old Times, Good old Times! Facts and Figures, Facts and Figures!
quotations.context: After the gentlemen leave, the bells ring and Trotty hears in them what he has just been told.
quotations.analysis: Each gentleman supplies one phrase, and the bells double each one the way a peal repeats its changes. 'If they said anything they said this', the narrator adds, which places the words in Trotty's ear and leaves the bells' own meaning open. By the Second Quarter his trot has fallen into the same measure and 'would fit itself to nothing else'.

quotations.text: You needn’t trouble yourself to think about anything. I will think for you; I know what is good for you; I am your perpetual parent.
quotations.speaker: Sir Joseph Bowley
quotations.context: Sir Joseph explains his system to Trotty in the library of his town house.
quotations.analysis: Paternalism is stated here with no disguise at all. The clauses move from thinking to knowing to being a parent, and 'perpetual' means that Trotty is never to grow up. A few sentences later Sir Joseph names the one lesson the poor require as 'entire Dependence on myself', and Trotty, listening, begins to feel more comfortable.

quotations.text: I only want to live like one of the Almighty’s creeturs. I can’t—I don’t—and so there’s a pit dug between me, and them that can and do.
quotations.speaker: Will Fern
quotations.context: Fern talks to Trotty in an alley after hearing what Sir Joseph has written about him.
quotations.analysis: Fern asks for nothing beyond what any creature has, and 'I can't—I don't' shows him correcting a complaint into a plain statement of fact. The pit between him and 'them that can and do' is the gap the gentlemen have been talking across all day without seeing it. He adds that men like him could be counted 'by hundreds and by thousands'.

quotations.text: ‘Unnatural and cruel!’ Toby cried. ‘Unnatural and cruel! None but people who were bad at heart, born bad, who had no business on the earth, could do such deeds. It’s too true, all I’ve heard to-day; too just, too full of proof. We’re Bad!’
quotations.speaker: Trotty
quotations.context: Alone by the fire, Trotty reads in his newspaper of a woman who killed herself and her young child.
quotations.analysis: Almost every phrase is borrowed. 'Born bad' is his own doubt from the morning, 'no business on the earth' is what the gentlemen have said all day, and 'too full of proof' accepts Filer's method. An hour after sheltering Fern and Lilian, Trotty still judges the woman in the paper by other men’s rules, and the bells answer him immediately.

quotations.text: ‘The voice of Time,’ said the Phantom, ‘cries to man, Advance! Time is for his advancement and improvement; for his greater worth, his greater happiness, his better life; his progress onward to that goal within its knowledge and its view, and set there, in the period when Time and He began.
quotations.speaker: The Goblin of the Great Bell
quotations.context: The Goblin's first charge against Trotty in the belfry.
quotations.analysis: Here Time is a machine that only goes forward: whoever tries to hold it back, the Goblin continues, 'arrests a mighty engine which will strike the meddler dead'. Its next charge makes a lament for 'days which have had their trial and their failure' a wrong done to the bells, which turns the red-faced gentleman's good old times into an offence, and Trotty, who half believed him, into an accessory.

quotations.text: Learn from her life, a living truth. Learn from the creature dearest to your heart, how bad the bad are born.
quotations.speaker: The Goblin of the Great Bell
quotations.context: Trotty hears Meg's voice in a dirge and thinks she is dead. The Bell tells him she is alive.
quotations.analysis: Trotty hears a promise that Meg will prove the gentlemen right. The vision shows the opposite, how a good woman is pressed towards a bad act, so the sentence is ironic in a way only the ending can confirm. 'From the creature dearest to your heart' comes back in the Fourth Quarter as the bells drive him after her, and at the river he answers it: 'I have learnt it'.

quotations.text: Strike me old, Meg! Wither me, and shrivel me, and free me from the dreadful thoughts that tempt me in my youth!
quotations.speaker: Lilian
quotations.context: In the vision, the grown Lilian and Meg sew together in a poor room for bare bread.
quotations.analysis: Lilian asks for age as protection, because her youth and looks are the one thing she has that someone would pay for. Dickens never names the temptation, and the next time she is heard of she is sending Meg money through Richard. 'Wither' and 'shrivel' treat her beauty as a danger, which is how Cute spoke of Meg's when he warned Trotty she was 'much too handsome'.

quotations.text: ‘Oh the brain, the brain!’ exclaimed the pious Alderman, lifting up his hands. ‘Oh the nerves, the nerves; the mysteries of this machine called Man! Oh the little that unhinges it: poor creatures that we are!
quotations.speaker: Alderman Cute
quotations.context: At Bowley Hall, Mr Fish tells Cute that Deedles the banker has shot himself in his own counting house.
quotations.analysis: For a rich man's suicide Cute finds nerves, the brain and 'this machine called Man', and says he will wear the deepest mourning. The narrator's adjective 'pious' is sarcastic. A paragraph later the narrator asks where the Putting Down has gone, and tells him to weigh this death against a starving mother's on the same scales.

quotations.text: Give us, in mercy, better homes when we’re a-lying in our cradles; give us better food when we’re a-working for our lives; give us kinder laws to bring us back when we're a-going wrong; and don’t set jail, jail, jail, afore us, everywhere we turn.
quotations.speaker: Will Fern
quotations.context: Fern, just out of prison, speaks to Sir Joseph's guests at the New Year's Day banquet.
quotations.analysis: After a list of arrests, each ending 'To jail with him', Fern turns to what could be done instead, and his order follows a life: the cradle, the working years, the moment of going wrong. 'Jail, jail, jail' is his reply to Cute's 'Put Down'. Among his hearers are 'you gentlemen that sits at Sessions', and Sir Joseph's response is to call him a living example.

quotations.text: ‘This is the last night of an Old Year, and I won’t carry ill-blood and quarrellings and disturbances into a New One, to please you nor anybody else,’ said Tugby, who was quite a retail Friend and Father.
quotations.speaker: Tugby
quotations.context: Tugby, standing in his shop doorway, refuses to let Meg and her baby back in.
quotations.analysis: Sir Joseph's title travels down the social scale to a small shopkeeper who was once his porter. 'Retail' is a shop word, and the joke has a serious point: the habit of mind needs no fortune, only a doorway to stand in. Tugby even echoes Sir Joseph's rule about carrying nothing into the New Year, and Meg goes from his door towards the river.

quotations.text: ‘Have mercy on her!’ he exclaimed, ‘as one in whom this dreadful crime has sprung from Love perverted; from the strongest, deepest Love we fallen creatures know! Think what her misery must have been, when such seed bears such fruit! Heaven meant her to be good. There is no loving mother on the earth who might not come to this, if such a life had gone before.
quotations.speaker: Trotty
quotations.context: At the river's edge, Trotty pleads with the figures in the bells for Meg.
quotations.analysis: This reverses his judgement of the Second Quarter almost phrase by phrase. The mother in the newspaper was 'unnatural and cruel'; the same act now springs from 'the strongest, deepest Love'. 'Heaven meant her to be good' is the book's answer to the question of whether the poor are born bad, and the last sentence extends the plea from Meg to every mother in her position.

quotations.text: If it be so, O listener, dear to him in all his visions, try to bear in mind the stern realities from which these shadows come; and in your sphere—none is too wide, and none too limited for such an end—endeavour to correct, improve, and soften them.
quotations.context: The last paragraph, just after the narrator asks whether Trotty dreamed.
quotations.analysis: Having left open whether the vision was a dream, the narrator insists that what it was drawn from is real. The request is modest and practical, and the parenthesis says no reader's position is too grand or too small to count. The book began by asking for an understanding between story-teller and story-reader, and it ends by giving the reader a job.

timeline.label: Malthus's Essay on the Principle of Population
timeline.detail: The argument that population outruns food, and that the poor should put off marriage, stands behind Filer's claim that Meg and Richard have no business to marry.

timeline.label: Dickens born in Portsmouth
timeline.detail: His family's later debts, and his own months of factory work as a boy, gave him first-hand knowledge of the poverty the gentlemen in The Chimes discuss from a distance.

timeline.label: Poor Law Amendment Act
timeline.detail: Parishes were grouped into Unions with workhouses. Will Fern keeps Lilian out of the Union twenty-eight miles from his home, where his own father was taken when he could no longer work.

timeline.label: A Christmas Carol published
timeline.detail: Dickens's first Christmas book appeared on 19 December and set the pattern The Chimes follows: a single night, supernatural visitors and a waking change.

timeline.label: Dickens moves his family to Genoa
timeline.detail: He wrote The Chimes there in the autumn, and his letters from the city mention the bells he heard.

timeline.label: Readings to friends before publication
timeline.detail: Dickens came back to London to correct proofs and read the new book aloud to friends. Daniel Maclise drew one of these readings, in John Forster's rooms, in pencil.

timeline.label: The Chimes published
timeline.detail: Issued on 16 December as the second of Dickens's Christmas books.

timeline.label: The Cricket on the Hearth
timeline.detail: The third Christmas book, a domestic story with far less politics in it.

timeline.label: The Battle of Life
timeline.detail: The fourth Christmas book, a love story set on the site of an old battlefield.

timeline.label: The Haunted Man and the Ghost's Bargain
timeline.detail: The fifth and last of the Christmas books, published on 19 December.

timeline.label: Dickens dies at Gad's Hill
timeline.detail: He died at his house in Kent on 9 June.

timeline.label: Forster's bequest
timeline.detail: John Forster's library and papers, including the manuscript of The Chimes, passed to the South Kensington Museum, now the Victoria and Albert Museum.

places.name: City of London
places.note: Trotty's church is never named. Cute expects to speak of Sir Joseph's son in the Common Council, and the banker Deedles is high in office in the Goldsmiths' Company, which puts the gentlemen's world in the City.

places.name: The Thames
places.note: The book calls it only 'the River', the place in the vision where Meg goes with her baby on the last night of the year.

places.name: Dorset
places.note: Lilian's mother died in Dorsetshire, the detail that lets Mrs Chickenstalker recognise the child in the last pages.

places.name: Genoa
places.note: Dickens was living here in 1844 and wrote The Chimes in the city.

places.name: Lincoln's Inn Fields
places.note: John Forster's rooms, where Dickens read the story to friends before publication and Maclise drew the scene.

places.name: Victoria and Albert Museum
places.note: The manuscript of The Chimes is kept here in the Forster Collection.

criticalViews.position: An answer to the political economists
criticalViews.summary: Read against the 1840s, the book replies to particular arguments. Filer speaks for a Malthusian economics that told the poor to put off marriage; Alderman Cute was taken as a portrait of Sir Peter Laurie, a City alderman who had said he would put down suicide; and the red-faced gentleman's good old times mock a nostalgia for the paternal England that Sir Joseph tries to practise.
criticalViews.counter: It proposes no measure of its own. Will Fern asks for better homes, food and laws in general terms, and the plot is settled inside one family on one night.

criticalViews.position: A vision the ending takes back
criticalViews.summary: Some readers find the waking too complete. Meg's ruin, Lilian's death and Richard's collapse are cancelled by a band and a pitcher of flip, and the argument can seem weaker once none of it has happened.
criticalViews.counter: The last paragraph meets the objection. It admits the whole may have been a dream and asks the reader to remember the 'stern realities' the shadows came from.

criticalViews.summary: A reading centred on Trotty treats the book as a study of how the poor take in their critics' view of them. The Goblin tries Trotty and never the gentlemen, and what he has to unlearn is his readiness to believe that people like him are born bad.
criticalViews.counter: That places the moral weight on the poorest man in the book, which sits awkwardly beside Fern's speech blaming homes, food and laws.

essayQuestions.question: How does Dickens present the gentlemen who talk about the poor in The Chimes?
plan: Introduce Filer, Cute, the red-faced gentleman and Sir Joseph as versions of one habit: discussing the poor in front of a poor man as if he were not there.
Show each made ridiculous by his own words: Filer's pennyweight of tripe, Cute's list of things to Put Down, Sir Joseph's 'perpetual parent'.
Examine the narrator's mock praise of Cute as a second voice that does the judging for the reader.
Trace the consequences in the vision: Richard persuaded he could do better, Fern jailed again and again, Meg turned out by a 'retail Friend and Father'.
Conclude on the Deedles episode, where Cute's response to a rich man's suicide exposes the double standard in his favourite phrase.

essayQuestions.question: 'Born bad.' How does The Chimes answer Trotty's question?
plan: Start with Trotty's doubt outside the church, and note that his 'we' is borrowed from the newspapers.
Show the gentlemen supplying an answer, and the newspaper story seeming to confirm it.
Read the Goblin's instruction to learn from Meg 'how bad the bad are born' as irony that the vision will unfold.
Follow Meg's decline and ask what the book blames at each stage: advice, wages, a husband's drinking, a landlord.
End at the river, where Trotty's plea for 'Love perverted' reverses his judgement of the mother in the paper.

essayQuestions.question: How does Dickens use time and the bells to shape The Chimes?
essayQuestions.focus: Structure, refrain and the New Year
plan: Explain the four Quarters and a frame that runs from noon to the midnight peal on the last day of the year.
Show the bells' words changing with Trotty's state of mind, from 'keep a good heart' to 'Put 'em down' to 'Follow her'.
Discuss the dying Old Year as an image of the aged labourer and the New Year as an infant heir.
Analyse the Goblin's speech on the voice of Time and its attack on the good old times.
Close with the New Year bells that end the vision and Trotty's prophecy of a sea of Time.

discussionQuestions: Trotty believes the gentlemen partly because they are gentlemen. What in the First Quarter makes their arguments sound convincing to him?
Will Fern speaks twice, once in an alley and once at a banquet. How has he changed between the two speeches, and why?
Alderman Cute is funny. Does the comedy make him less dangerous or more?
Meg's decline takes years in the vision. Which single event in it seems to you most responsible?
Does the happy waking weaken the book, or does the final paragraph rescue it?
The Spirit of the Chimes has Lilian's face as a child. Why might Dickens have chosen her as Trotty's guide?

related.why: The Christmas book of the year before, with the same shape: one night of supernatural instruction and a changed man at the end of it.
The last Christmas book, where the man in need of a lesson is a scholar and the lesson is about memory.
The Christmas book that followed in 1845, with the politics set aside and a household at the centre.
The Astor collection that prints The Chimes alongside three of the other Christmas books.
The customs, charity and seasonal print culture the Christmas books were written for.
